title: Frontend Development
description: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, accessibility, and modern component architecture — everything that runs in the browser.
blurb: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, accessibility, and modern component architecture — everything that runs in the browser.
careerApplications: Frontend roles and full-stack roles both expect this; even backend-focused engineers are expected to ship a usable UI.

lessons.title: HTML structure & semantics
objectives: Structure a page with semantic tags instead of generic divs
Explain how semantic HTML changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect semantic HTML with document structure and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: HTML gives content structure and meaning. Semantic tags — <header>, <nav>, <main>, <article>, <footer> — describe WHAT something is, not just how it looks, which helps screen readers, search engines, and other developers understand your page at a glance.
commonMistakes: 'Div soup' — building an entire layout from unlabeled <div>s when a semantic tag already exists for that role.
lessons.careerRelevance: Semantic HTML is often the first thing a code review or interview will flag on a frontend submission.
lessons.explain: HTML gives content structure and meaning. Semantic tags — <header>, <nav>, <main>, <article>, <footer> — describe WHAT something is, not just how it looks, which helps screen readers, search engines, and other developers understand your page at a glance.

lessons.title: CSS fundamentals: the box model & selectors
objectives: Explain the CSS box model
Write selectors with the right specificity
Explain how box model changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect box model with specificity and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Every element is a box: content, then padding, then border, then margin, from the inside out. CSS selectors target elements to style — by tag, class, id, or relationship (descendant, child) — and specificity determines which rule wins when several apply to the same element (id beats class beats tag).
commonMistakes: Fighting CSS with !important instead of understanding why a more specific selector is winning — it treats the symptom, not the cause.
lessons.careerRelevance: The box model is the single most load-bearing mental model in all of CSS.
lessons.explain: Every element is a box: content, then padding, then border, then margin, from the inside out. CSS selectors target elements to style — by tag, class, id, or relationship (descendant, child) — and specificity determines which rule wins when several apply to the same element (id beats class beats tag).

lessons.title: Responsive design: Flexbox, Grid, media queries
objectives: Build a layout that adapts to different screen sizes
Explain how Flexbox changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Flexbox with Grid and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Responsive design means one page works well from a phone to a desktop. Flexbox arranges items along one axis (great for navbars, button rows); Grid arranges in two dimensions (great for full page layouts).
commonMistakes: Designing desktop-first and bolting on mobile support later — it's far easier to design mobile-first and add complexity as the screen grows.
lessons.careerRelevance: Most real-world traffic is mobile; a design that breaks at 390px wide is a shipped bug, not an edge case.
lessons.explain: Responsive design means one page works well from a phone to a desktop. Flexbox arranges items along one axis (great for navbars, button rows); Grid arranges in two dimensions (great for full page layouts).

lessons.title: JavaScript & the DOM
objectives: Select, read, and modify DOM elements from JavaScript
Respond to user events
Explain how DOM changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect DOM with event listeners and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: The DOM (Document Object Model) is the live, in-memory tree of your page that JavaScript can read and change. `querySelector` finds elements; `addEventListener` reacts to clicks/input/etc; changing an element's `.textContent` or classes updates what the user sees, instantly, with no page reload.
commonMistakes: Directly manipulating dozens of elements ad hoc as an app grows — this is exactly the pain component frameworks (React etc.) exist to solve.
lessons.careerRelevance: DOM manipulation fundamentals underpin every frontend framework, even ones that abstract it away.
lessons.explain: The DOM (Document Object Model) is the live, in-memory tree of your page that JavaScript can read and change. `querySelector` finds elements; `addEventListener` reacts to clicks/input/etc; changing an element's `.textContent` or classes updates what the user sees, instantly, with no page reload.

lessons.title: React fundamentals: components, props & state
lessons.explain: React builds interfaces from components whose output depends on props and state. State changes trigger re-rendering, while effects are for synchronizing with work outside rendering such as network requests or browser APIs.
objectives: Build a small React component that manages its own state and reacts to a user event
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: useEffect for side effects, API data fetching, loading and error states.
Explain how components changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect components with JSX and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
commonMistakes: Mutating state directly (state.value = x) instead of calling the setter function (setValue(x)) -- React only re-renders when it detects an update through its own setter, not a raw mutation.
lessons.explanation: React builds interfaces from components whose output depends on props and state. State changes trigger re-rendering, while effects are for synchronizing with work outside rendering such as network requests or browser APIs.
lessons.careerRelevance: These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.

lessons.title: Accessibility (a11y) fundamentals
objectives: Apply the most common accessibility fixes: labels, alt text, contrast, keyboard nav
Explain how alt text changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect alt text with labels and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Accessibility means your site works for people using screen readers, keyboard-only navigation, or with visual impairments — not an afterthought, a requirement.
commonMistakes: Using a <div onclick=...> as a button — it looks like a button but is invisible to keyboard and screen-reader users, who have no way to activate it.
lessons.careerRelevance: Accessibility is a legal requirement in many jurisdictions and a frequent, explicit item in frontend code reviews.
lessons.explain: Accessibility means your site works for people using screen readers, keyboard-only navigation, or with visual impairments — not an afterthought, a requirement.

lessons.title: Modern frontend architecture: components & state
objectives: Explain component-based architecture and where state should live
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: client-side routing.
Explain how components changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect components with state and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Frontend architecture is about separating responsibilities so a growing UI stays understandable. Components own focused presentation or interaction responsibilities, props move information into components, composition builds larger views, and client-side routing maps URLs to application screens.
commonMistakes: Putting all state in one giant top-level component 'to be safe' — it works but makes every small change trigger unnecessary re-renders and coupling across the whole app.
lessons.careerRelevance: Component thinking is the baseline mental model for React, Vue, and virtually every modern frontend job. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.
lessons.explain: Frontend architecture is about separating responsibilities so a growing UI stays understandable. Components own focused presentation or interaction responsibilities, props move information into components, composition builds larger views, and client-side routing maps URLs to application screens.

exercises.title: Semantic refactor
exercises.prompt: Rewrite a div-only page layout using semantic tags (header, nav, main, footer).

exercises.title: Box model debug
exercises.prompt: Given a layout where padding is making an element overflow its container, explain the fix (box-sizing: border-box).

exercises.title: Responsive card grid
exercises.prompt: Build a 3-column card grid with CSS Grid that collapses to 1 column under 600px.

exercises.title: DOM todo toggle
exercises.prompt: Write JS that toggles a 'done' class on a list item when it's clicked.

exercises.title: Accessibility audit
exercises.prompt: Given a form with no labels and low-contrast text, list every fix needed and why.

exercises.title: Component split
exercises.prompt: Given a single 200-line page of markup, propose how you'd split it into 4-5 reusable components and what state each would own.

A <div onclick=...> used as a button is problematic mainly because:
In component architecture, state should generally live:
options: always in the very top-level component
as close as possible to where it's needed, lifted up only when shared
apply different CSS at different viewport widths
